title: Bigger Side of Zero
statement:
You get an array nums sorted in non-decreasing order. Count the strictly negative values and the strictly positive values. Return the larger of the two counts.

Zero is neither negative nor positive, so zeros are not counted on either side.

examples.why: Three negatives against two positives. The two zeros belong to neither side.
One negative, three positives. Duplicates each count.

constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: A linear count works. The sorted order lets you do better: where do the negatives end and the positives begin?
The negatives are everything before the first index whose value is ≥ 0. The positives are everything from the first index whose value is ≥ 1.
Write one lower-bound binary search and call it with 0 and with 1.

explain.intuition:
In a sorted array the negatives form a block at the front and the positives a block at the back, with any zeros between them. You only need the two boundaries.

A lower-bound search finds the first index whose value is at least some target. With target 0 that index equals the number of negatives. With target 1 it is where the positives start, so there are n − index of them. Two binary searches, O(log n) total.
steps: Write firstAtLeast(t): binary search over [0, n) for the first index with nums[i] ≥ t, returning n if none.
pitfalls: Counting zeros as positive, for example by searching for the first value ≥ 0 for both sides.
Searching for one boundary and assuming the other side is everything else; zeros in the middle break that.
Returning -1 from the search when nothing qualifies instead of n, which miscounts an all-negative array.

solutions.title: Count in one pass
solutions.idea: Walk the array and count each sign.

solutions.title: Two lower-bound searches
solutions.idea: The first index ≥ 0 is the count of negatives; the first index ≥ 1 marks where positives begin.

followups: The array is sorted in non-increasing order instead. What changes in the searches?
Answer many queries "how many values lie in [a, b]?" on the same sorted array.
